etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gowne, from Anglo-Norman goune, gune (“fur-trimmed coat, pelisse”), from Old French goune, from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment, a fur”). Cognate with Manx gooyn, Irish gúna.

definitions.definition: A woman's ordinary outer dress, such as a calico or silk gown.
The dress of civil officers, as opposed to military officers.
The official robe of certain professionals, clerics, and scholars, such as university students and officers, barristers, judges, etc.

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: VVhat is he an honeſt man? the deuill he is, he is the Parſon of the Towne,You thinke ther’s no knauerie hid vnder a black gowne,  […]

definitions.definition: (by metonymy) The university community, especially as contrasted with the local populace.
A loose wrapper worn by gentlemen within doors; a dressing gown.
Any sort of dress or garb.
The robe worn by a surgeon.
To dress in a gown, to don or garb with a gown.
